binders: There exists a real constant C.
Universally quantify over an arbitrary type Ω equipped with a measurable-space structure.
Universally quantify over a measure μ on Ω equipped with the assumption that μ is a probability measure.
Universally quantify over a real-valued function X : Ω → ℝ.
hypotheses: The exponential-moment gauge of X is finite, meaning it is strictly below ∞ in ENNReal.
conclusions: The exponential-moment gauge of the centered function ω ↦ X(ω) − ∫ X dμ is at most ENNReal.ofReal(C) times the exponential-moment gauge of X.
mathematical_definitions: For any real-valued function Y, its gauge is inf {t ∈ [0,∞] : Y is measurable, t ≠ 0, t ≠ ∞, exp(|Y|/t.toReal) is μ-integrable, and ∫ exp(|Y|/t.toReal) dμ ≤ 2}.
Since C ≥ 1, ENNReal.ofReal(C) is simply C viewed as an extended nonnegative real.
Because μ is a probability measure, ∫ X dμ is the expectation of X.
translation.proposition_plain_english: There is a single absolute real constant C ≥ 1 such that, on every probability space, every measurable real random variable X whose exponential absolute-value gauge is finite satisfies ‖X − E[X]‖ ≤ C‖X‖, where ‖Y‖ is the infimum over positive finite t for which exp(|Y|/t) is integrable and has expectation at most 2.

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: The statement is only for real-valued functions and probability measures.
It assumes pointwise Borel measurability of X, not merely almost-everywhere measurability.
Only X with finite gauge are covered; functions for which the admissible-scale set is empty have gauge equal to the top element and are excluded by this hypothesis.

The target does not separately assume that X is integrable before writing ∫X dμ; integrability is expected to follow mathematically from finite exponential gauge, but that implication is not itself encoded as a premise.
The gauge is an infimum of admissible scales, so the infimum itself need not be an admissible scale.
The constant is existential and no explicit numerical value or optimality assertion is encoded.
The gauge may equal zero in degenerate cases; then the conclusion requires the centered gauge to be zero as well rather than becoming vacuous.

The centering uses the library's total Bochner integral term; the dossier does not expose its behavior on nonintegrable functions, though the finite-gauge hypothesis is intended to rule that case out.
ambiguities: The one-level body shown for the integral is an opaque wrapper projection, so its totalization convention outside the integrable domain is not recoverable from this dossier alone.

The dossier does not state whether the infimum-defined gauge has already been proved equivalent to any named norm or tail/moment characterization; the translation therefore uses only the displayed exponential-integral definition.
